key_insight: The paper shows that driving policies can appear safe by exploiting simulator permissiveness with abrupt, uncomfortable maneuvers. It introduces an adaptive way to define action spaces so the policy stays within comfort bounds while still learning effectively.
problem_solved: It addresses the mismatch between simulator action grids and real vehicle comfort, where learned policies can game safety metrics by producing unrealistic accelerations and jerks. The goal is to make safety evaluation reflect genuine driving quality rather than simulator loopholes.
method: Replace fixed action grids with comfort-bounded, adaptive action spaces tied to realized vehicle dynamics.
Constrain actions so resulting accelerations and jerks remain within human-comfort limits.
Use adaptation to preserve learning flexibility while preventing last-second, high-aggression maneuvers that inflate metrics.
impact: This matters because it makes reinforcement-learned driving policies more realistic, robust, and occupant-friendly. For practitioners, it improves the credibility of simulator results and reduces the risk of deploying policies that only look safe in simulation.
visual_elements: Before/after comparison of fixed-grid actions vs adaptive comfort-bounded actions
Diagram showing commanded actions versus realized acceleration/jerk trajectories
A safety-metric chart illustrating inflated simulator scores from abrupt maneuvers
Icon set for comfort, safety, and realism in driving policy evaluation
paper_title: Comfort by Construction: Adaptive, Comfort-Bounded Action Spaces for Learned Driving Policies
paper_authors: Anna Rothenhäusler, Daniel Jost, Raghu Rajan, Faris Janjos, Oliver Scheel
